Speaking to Sky Sports, the Sunderland man stated: “I think the wind played a massive part and credit to both defences and the attacks as well to be able to keep it to no goals in that swirling wind.

“I think it was a good effort from everybody so obviously we want three points from where we are in the table but keep putting up the performances like that and we’ll get some.

“As a defender it’s always nice to have a clean sheet and especially after the last few games where we haven’t had one.

Sources indicate that “It’s always something we’re looking to do and Robin [Roefs] came up with some massive saves, Omar [Alderete] coming on was really good as well and I hope my teammate’s [Nordi Mukiele] OK as well because I think that was kind of my fault. But we got the clean sheet for him so hopefully not too bad.”.

When asked about Sunderland being bottom of the league, he replied: “I think always the table reflects fairly where teams deserve to be, and I think over the course of the course of the season if we keep putting in performances like that it will represent where we should be.

“But the table always reflects where people should be but we need to keep looking at ourselves, don’t look at other anyone else, it’s no-one else’s fault but us and we know that.”.

That result means that Sunderland’s stay bottom of the Premier League and without a win in the competition since August 30, while Leeds earn their fifth draw in eight top-flight fixtures to move up to seventh on 11 points.

Sunderland were warned about “second season syndrome” and shrugged them off in the summer as they looked forward to their first European campaign for more than 50 years.

They had dismissed the gloomy pre-season predictions the previous year and had gone on to enjoy their most successful season in the top flight since the heady days of the Peter Reid era at the start of the century.

So when the “experts” told them it would be much harder this season—that they would no longer have the element of surprise and the squad would be badly stretched by the extra games in the Europa League—it was easy to ignore.

You cannot blame them. It has been a magical couple of years on Wearside where everything has gone in their favour, but reality has hit hard this season.

Sunderland are bottom of the table heading into this home game against Leeds United and have not won in the league since August.

The limp defeat at Bournemouth last weekend brought things to a head, with defender Nordi Mukiele suggesting in a post match interview that his teammates had become arrogant and had forgotten how hard they had to work last season to be successful.

There was a better performance and a decent draw away to Lech Poznan on Thursday night but Regis Le Bris’ side desperately need a win in the league.

Leeds United have been one of the story’s of the season so far and have looked dangerous in every game so far.

Recent findings suggest that the return to fitness of Brian Brobbey is a big boost for Sunderland, but I don’t think any side would like to face Leeds at the moment. The home crowd will be anxious.

Régis Le Bris has made three changes to his Sunderland side.

Brian Brobbey returns to the starting line-up after recovering from a hamstring injury, while Luke O’Nien and Nilson Angulo also come into the side.

Omar Alderete and Timur Tutierov are named among the substitutes, while Kevin Danso begins a one-match suspension following his red card at Bournemouth.

Manager Daniel Farke has made three changes to his starting line-up.

In a recent development, jaka Bijol replaces Nico Elvedi and starts alongside Tarik Muharemovic and James Justin. Brenden Aaronson and Harry Wilson both start in place of Anton Stach and Noah Okafor, supporting Dominic Calvert-Lewin in the Leeds United attack.

Leeds United: Trafford, Justin, Bijol, Muharemović, Bogle, Ampadu, Tanaka, Gudmundsson, Wilson, Aaronson, Calvert-LewinSubs: Zetterer, Bard, Longstaff, Stach, Gruev, Cresswell, Nmecha, Okafor, Bahoya.

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of this Premier League match between Sunderland and Leeds United at the Stadium of Light.

The final game of this gameweek sees these two Northern giants lock horns once again in a very intriguing encounter, with Sunderland especially in need of three points.

In a recent development, following their opening season back in the Premier League last term, Sunderland enjoyed a historic campaign, placing seventh to qualify for European competition for the first time in 53 years. Therefore, their workload for the 2025-26 season has increased, which has caused their domestic form to suffer.

Sunderland currently find themselves bottom of the top-flight table, with just one win and four points from their opening seven league matches. They’ve lost their previous four Premier League games, but a win here could lift them out of the drop zone, depending on other results at Old Trafford and Selhurst Park.

Industry observers note that meanwhile, in the Europa League, it’s a completely different story. Regis Le Bris’ side are unbeaten, earning seven points from the first nine available. They drew 1-1 with Polish outfit Lech Poznan on Thursday evening, and given the relentless juggling act of domestic and European football, they’re already back in today against a very well-drilled team.

Industry observers note that leeds have made a solid start to the season and find themselves eighth in the Premier League, having only lost one match — a narrow 2-1 defeat to Arsenal at the Emirates earlier this month. Last time out, Daniel Farke’s side drew 1-1 with Manchester United at Elland Road, meaning they’re still searching for a first Premier League win since September 14.

Sources indicate that speaking in his preview, Farke noted: “To win any point in this league, you always have to be on it. And you always have to be close to be perfect, especially for normal sides - not like the top two. And for that, we are very respectful. So we don’t go into the trap and think we are bigger than we are. We are just the second year back on Premier League level. And we fight for every point.”.

Published: 15:33 EST, 20 November 2026 | Updated: 15:36 EST, 20 November 2026.

Rangers goalkeeper Ivor Pandur has revealed his 'unbelievable' experience of working under Allan McGregor.

The former Rangers, Hull and Scotland keeper was brought into the Ibrox backroom staff by Derek McInnes as lead goalkeeping coach in the summer.

Pandur is reaping the benefits of his mentor’s experience and their relationship having kept eight clean sheets during his team’s 12-match unbeaten run.

'It’s unbelievable,' noted the Croatian ahead of the Premiership encounter at Motherwell on Saturday night.

'With the career that he had here, he obviously has a lot of experience.

In a recent development, 'We have a great relationship where he is my coach, he is my friend. So he’ll tell me when I ask him if I can do something better.

Ivor Pandur has made an impressive start to life at Rangers after joining from Hull City.

'We are here to make each other better. If I can make him a better coach, that’s brilliant. But he’s making me a better goalkeeper and I’m really, really thankful for that.

'Training, first of all, is really, really enjoyable. And he always asks, "What do I want to do? What do I want to improve?". And he’ll give me feedback.

It has been revealed that 'There’s not a single thing, I would say, that made me better. Just in general, to be able to work in these kind of circumstances and conditions, it’s really enjoyable and it’s making me happy every day.

It has been revealed that 'It’s making me excited to come to work. And that’s because of him also.

'He’s a great guy and he was a great goalkeeper, and it’s enough for me to learn from.'.

Manager McInnes this week described Pandur as a key 'driver' of team culture off the pitch, citing the respect he has from his team-mates.

Pandur, who joined from Hull in the summer, said: 'I always want to lead by example. The words are not so important if you’re not doing your job right.

'So if I can lead by example and show up every day, work as hard as I can, a lot of young players can see that.

Pandur insists he is only going to keep improving under the guidance of Allan McGregor.

In a recent development, 'And obviously, I’m always there to help somebody. I was also 19 or 20 and, when I had somebody to learn from, it was much easier.

'Because you get experiences through life and through years of playing, I always try to help everybody else.

'So there are times where I can be more vocal if I feel a need for it, but it’s never my first objective. It’s always to lead by example.'.

Pandur is still awaiting his first international cap but was again away with Croatia this month and he feels meeting the demands of Rangers fans is getting the best out of him.

Industry observers note that 'It keeps you on your toes,” the former Rijeka, Hellas Verona and Fortuna Sittard player noted. 'But in my opinion, pressure is in your head.

Industry observers note that 'We all play the game we love and we try to do our best. Some days you’ll do good, some days you’ll do bad. We always try to do the right thing.

'Pressure is bigger here, there’s more followers. But it can only make you better because it gets everything out of you.'.

Iran war oil shock drives dip in global emissions, study highlights

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (461 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Global carbon emissions are set to slightly drop this year, a new study suggests, largely as a result of high energy prices in the wake of the US war on Iran and the disruption of supply through the Strait of Hormuz.
  • Emissions from oil, gas and coal are the main drivers of climate change.
  • "It's downwards, which sounds good, but this is largely driven by the war in Iran, what's happened in the Strait of Hormuz," stated the study's co-author Glen Peters, a scientist at the CICERO Center for International Climate Research in Norway.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Global carbon emissions are set to slightly drop this year, a new study suggests, largely as a result of high energy prices in the wake of the US war on Iran and the disruption of supply through the Strait of Hormuz.

Emissions from oil, gas and coal are the main drivers of climate change. While over the past decade, these emissions have risen by 0.9% per year, they are expected to drop by 0.4% in 2026.

"It's downwards, which sounds good, but this is largely driven by the war in Iran, what's happened in the Strait of Hormuz," stated the study's co-author Glen Peters, a scientist at the CICERO Center for International Climate Research in Norway.

"So in a way, a little bit of good news, but for the wrong reasons.".

The study was released while global leaders are meeting in Turkey for the United Nations' COP31 climate conference.

Industry observers note that the study published by international research group the Global Carbon Project found that oil emissions dropped by 1.9% in 2026, while natural gas fell by 0.3%. Coal emissions however continued to rise, by around 0.6%.

"A drop in emissions in ‌one year is not a peak unless it ‌is driven ​by structural change," Peters cautioned.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

A structural change would mean that emissions would slowly rise to a peak and then slowly decline afterward, indicating a long term trend. That's not what happened though, Peters mentioned. "What we see this year is [that] oil emissions are going up and then suddenly, bang, down 2%.".

It is the third time in recent years that global carbon pollution has dropped. The previous declines were during the global economic crisis in 2009 and during the COVID pandemic in 2020. In each of those cases, emissions went back up once global economies recovered.

Recent findings suggest that while the geopolitical shocks of the past year have been the driving factors behind the temporary emissions reversal, there has also been a rise in renewable energy contributing to the data. So while solar panels, wind farms and electric vehicles did make a difference, they were just not enough to cut emissions by themselves.

"The long-term answer remains the rapid deployment of clean energy technologies," according to co-author of the study, Pierre Friedlingstein, of the Global Carbon Budget Office at the University.

And even though emissions from fossil fuels dropped slightly, overall global carbon dioxide emissions still went up by about 1%, the study warns. The overall rise is because of land use changes like deforestation and peat fires, which increased too fast to be offset by the slight decrease in fossil fuel burning.

#48682. Breaking: Microbiome home tests are taking off. Can they be trusted?

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2500 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nature ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Microbiome home tests are taking off. Can they be trusted?

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2500 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A mix of microorganisms from a human faecal sample, imaged using a scanning electron microscope.
  • First, the good news: I have 133 microbial species living in my gut.
  • Revealed: how this common gut microbe protects against heart disease.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A mix of microorganisms from a human faecal sample, imaged using a scanning electron microscope. Credit: Steve Gschmeissner/Science Photo Library.

First, the good news: I have 133 microbial species living in my gut. That’s a collection that ranks as ‘excellent’ according to NirvanaBiome, the company in Germantown, Maryland, that analysed my stool sample. The firm based its rating on the overall diversity of my gut’s residents plus my levels of specific beneficial and undesirable species.

Revealed: how this common gut microbe protects against heart disease.

Revealed: how this common gut microbe protects against heart disease.

But then came a second, less promising assessment: Viome in Bellevue, Washington, identified only 61 kinds of active microorganism in my gut and suggested that some of them were not performing optimally. Viome recommended dietary changes and offered customized supplements to improve my health.

I was intrigued by the results, but also flummoxed by the different messages. That’s not an uncommon response, says microbiologist Rob Knight, director of the Center for Microbiome Innovation at the University of California, San Diego. When scientists tested a handful of microbiome testing kits alongside one another in formal studies, they found wide discrepancies in the results. These differences make it hard to understand or really trust the findings from any given provider, says Diane Hoffmann, director of the Law and Health Care programme at the University of Maryland in Baltimore, who co-authored one of those studies.

Industry observers note that the companies stand by their products. “Of course there’s variability,” says Kelly Moffat, chief operations officer for Cmbio in Germantown, which does the laboratory work and genetic sequencing for NirvanaBiome. “There has to be because this is complex testing.”.

Momo Vuyisich, chief science officer at Viome’s lab in Bothwell, Washington, also states he was unsurprised by the degree of variation found by formal studies. Labs use different methods to extract, sequence and analyse microbial genetic material. Viome, for example, sequences RNA rather than DNA, allowing it to uncover microbial gene activity, rather than only the presence of genes. Vuyisich argues that this is more relevant to human health. And he says that although every method will have biases, as long as a consumer sticks with the same provider, it should produce results that are comparable over time.

Interest in these kinds of test is booming. “There’s so much public enthusiasm and excitement about the microbiome,” says Knight. Some customers are simply curious about the microscopic beings that live inside them and potentially affect their health; others have health conditions such as irritable bowel syndrome and hope that their gut microbes will reveal the underlying cause or a path to better health.

According to recent reports, although people can order the tests and follow their recommendations without the help of a medical professional, some people are bringing the findings to their physicians. “I groan when I see someone come in with a microbiome test,” says Fergus Shanahan, a gastroenterologist and immunologist at University College Cork in Ireland, who has spent much of his career studying the microbiome. For someone struggling with gut health, a consumer microbiome profile isn’t usually specific enough to help. And if there’s a concern about an infection, such as Clostridioides difficile, it’s more straightforward to test for known pathogens than to assess the entire microbial community.

The tantalizing links between gut microbes and the brain.

The tantalizing links between gut microbes and the brain.

Microbiologists and gasteroenterologists who spoke to Nature generally agreed that microbiome testing has the potential to both reflect and promote health, but many stated that the science isn’t yet mature enough to support microbiome testing for most consumers. In their view, the limited clinical usefulness of today’s consumer tests can make them poor value for money (costing around US$100–300). The specialists warn that acting on advice that doesn’t come from clinicians could lead customers to adopt unnecessarily restrictive diets or delay appropriate medical assessment. Critics say that consumer microbiome testing needs more regulatory scrutiny and oversight.

Recent findings suggest that “This is an industry that’s running wild,” states genomicist Jacques Ravel, director of the Center for Advanced Microbiome Research and Innovation at the University of Maryland School of Medicine in Baltimore and a co-author on one of the studies that tested several providers. With regards to testing methods, he says, “there’s no standard”.

Moffat states, “I think the jury’s out on exactly what it is that we can actionably do today based on this data.” But she says that microbiome profiles, combined with other testing such as gut metabolomics, could yield interesting and useful health information.

The gut microbiome has emerged as an incredible correlate of overall health. From immune-system function to metabolism, skin disorders and mental health, study after study has found links between a person’s well-being and the trillions of microbes that live in their digestive tract. The premise of a head count of these species and assessment of their actions, to monitor and improve gut health in a personalized way, certainly sounds appealing. Viome’s website, for example, promises: “No more trial and error … Follow a plan built precisely for you.”.

Companies can identify species and, on the basis of those lists, infer what the microbes are probably doing, such as manufacturing metabolites or inciting inflammation. But running even the simplest microbiome testing is expensive, indicates Alessandra Cervino, research director at PiLeJe, a science-based food-supplement firm in Paris. She says her microbiome testing company, Luxia Scientific, closed in 2024 for financial reasons.

Some microbiome testing firms recommend fermented foods, such as kombucha, for gut health.Credit: Deb Lindsey for The Washington Post via Getty.

Many testing companies also offer lifestyle and nutritional advice or sell supplements. For example, Viome analysed diverse functions performed by the microbes in my gut, such as digestive efficiency, gas production and serotonin manufacture. I then received a detailed eating blueprint — which told me to eschew broccoli and load up on pecans, among other suggestions — along with an offer for precision supplements and probiotics with a price tag of more than $150 a month. Although it’s hard to change the composition of microbes in one’s gut, alterations in diet or even simply ageing can shift their activities, states Vuyisich. The tech giant recommends re-testing every four to six months to check for shifts and upgrade the plan.

According to recent reports, he points to 19 peer-reviewed publications by Viome as evidence of the tech giant’s rigour (see go.nature.com/4actdhq). For example, the firm’s analysis for consumers is supported, in part, by published data on how gut microbes influence individuals’ responses to glucose in various foods, based on 550 people in the United States who collectively ate more than 30,000 meals while wearing glucose monitors1. The company validated those findings in a further cohort in Japan, Vuyisich notes, but those data are not published.

Industry observers note that microbiome tests are not created equal, says Tim Spector, a physician-scientist at King’s College London and co-founder of London-based ZOE, which offers microbiome testing and a supplement in addition to a gut-health app that I’ve been playing with. ZOE’s products, Spector says, are backed by research on thousands of people. “There definitely are some not-so-good players out there that give this field a bad name,” he says. “It’s not easy to do this well.”.

Industry observers note that there are also several ways to do microbe testing; companies take varying approaches that yield disparate results, as at least two studies have shown. Scientists at the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) in Gaithersburg, Maryland, shipped homogenized stool samples from one person to seven companies2. NIST’s remit is researching and applying standards for measurement. This experiment was a step towards understanding the diversity of testing options out there, says one of the study authors, NIST microbiologist Stephanie Servetas, who is based in Sheridan, Wyoming. The researchers didn’t name the companies in their report because they wanted to focus attention on the comparison between tests rather than perceived accuracy of any individual provider.

The result: “Companies produce strikingly different results,” says co-author Scott Jackson, a molecular geneticist who used to direct the NIST microbiology program and is now a consultant in Saint Michaels, Maryland. “They couldn’t even agree on what’s healthy and unhealthy,” Jackson says. The microbe lists ranged from 34 to 906 identified genera; only 3 of which highlighted up in all reports. In fact, the results were as varied from company to company as they would be for different people, despite all tests being done on samples from the same individual.

Recent findings suggest that A European and Canadian team obtained similar outcomes when they sent homogenized samples from one person’s stool to six companies, also anonymized. Three companies rated the microbial diversity as “excellent” or “good”; two called it “average”; one said it was “unfavourable”3. The results were so variable, that at least some of them must be lacking in validation or standardization, says co-author Céline Druart, executive director of the Pharmabiotic Research Institute (PRI) in Brussels, a non-profit organization specializing in regulation of microbiome innovations. “It’s very difficult to make a conclusion,” she says.

How gut bacteria could boost cancer treatments.

How gut bacteria could boost cancer treatments.

This broad divergence in results is not surprising, indicates Jack Gilbert, director of the Microbiome and Metagenomics Center at the University of California, San Diego. The variation starts at sampling: scoop a bit of faecal matter into a tube, stab it with a coring device or swipe the sampler across some used toilet paper; ship it off as-is, or in some kind of preservative (as both Viome’s and NirvanaBiome’s kits asked me to). Each option could influence the balance of the microbes that are collected and what survives to be sequenced.

Recent findings suggest that in the lab, Servetas says the method by which the researchers extract genetic material from a sample is a big source of divergence. Gentler protocols will bias a sample towards microbes that are easy to crack open, whereas harsher methods will capture a higher share of species with tougher exteriors.

After sequencing, another major source of difference, says Knight, is the bioinformatics pipeline that labs use. What length or number of genetic sequences is required to consider a microbe present? What list of sequences and microbes are they using as a reference? “All bets are off when you then computationally analyse it with your favourite method,” says Knight.

Would companies support having standards to validate their tests? “We are really big advocates on really having a standard here,” indicates Kimberley Sukhum, chief science officer at Tiny Health in Austin, Texas, which offers gut microbiome tests as well as vaginal microbiome tests.

But it’s hard to set those standards, in part because there is no known ‘ground truth’ for a natural microbial sample. Compare that with, say, a blood-glucose test; a lab can get a known value from a standard sample either right or wrong. But the microbiome, in its glorious complexity, does not allow for such simple validation. NIST has used mixed human donor samples to develop a standard4. And Tiny Health has experimented with generating a reference for benchmarking from synthetic communities. It was built from individual microbial species rather than sampled from faeces5. But neither of those standards is exactly like the microbiome of an individual person.

Sources indicate that even if labs could assess a microbiome perfectly, they’d still have a problem: there’s no defined healthy microbiome like there is one range of healthy blood-glucose levels. Each person’s microbiome is unique, like a fingerprint. There are infinitely many ways to have a healthy microbiome, and infinitely many ways to have an unhealthy one, says Shanahan; it’s not entirely clear how to draw a line between the two.

How gut microbes could drive brain disorders.

How gut microbes could drive brain disorders.

Companies must compare customer microbiomes with some standard of health, but these vary too. They might be based on past customers or large, public databases. But microbiomes differ considerably depending on factors such as ethnicity, sex, age, recent antibiotic use or even whether someone was born by caesarean section.

Breaking: Gattuso: ‘Feel like I’ve been at Lazio for 10 years, Frattesi is fine’

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gennaro Gattuso states he feels at home at Lazio and that it feels like he has been with the club for 10 years rather than six months, and has provided a detailed revision on his list of injuries and fitness concerns, declaring Davide Frattesi fit to play against Lecce on Saturday.
  • Lazio return to Serie A action at home against Lecce on Saturday at 14.00 GMT.
  • Up next for Gattuso and his players is a visit from Lecce, who sit in 14th ahead of kick-off with 10 points to their name from their first 11 games of the season.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gennaro Gattuso states he feels at home at Lazio and that it feels like he has been with the club for 10 years rather than six months, and has provided a detailed revision on his list of injuries and fitness concerns, declaring Davide Frattesi fit to play against Lecce on Saturday.

Lazio return to Serie A action at home against Lecce on Saturday at 14.00 GMT. The Biancocelesti went into the international break sat alone at the top of the Serie A standings, one of two sides still unbeaten in the league after 11 matches, and they have only dropped points twice since the beginning of the 2026-27 campaign.

Up next for Gattuso and his players is a visit from Lecce, who sit in 14th ahead of kick-off with 10 points to their name from their first 11 games of the season.

Gattuso sat down for his pre-match press conference ahead of the Lecce clash on Friday afternoon.

Gattuso’s press conference began with a detailed revision on Lazio’s injured players and those who have recently returned from international duty.

“I don’t have to assess Frattesi, he spent the whole week with the group, he’s fine. We’ll see whether he has a cold or something later today, but everything else he has done has been fine.

“The Danes arrived the day after their game at 18.30 and worked in the gym along with Belahyane and Dele-Bashiru. We worked at a low intensity yesterday but everybody worked as a team. I’m also talking about some of the injured players. Zaccagni has been working on the pitch for the last five or six days. He still has some swelling, but he’s at a good speed and we’ll see him next week.

According to recent reports, “Nuno [Tavares] has started rehab in the pool along with Sutalo. Adam [Marusic] had a small relapse on the concern he had a month ago. We’ll be able to assess the condition of the injured players next week. Cataldi didn’t train yesterday due to a minor discomfort in his adductor. We don’t think it’s anything serious.”.

Gattuso was asked how he looks on managing this next block of fixtures in the lead-up to Christmas.

He insisted: “We’re only thinking about tomorrow’s game. We’re facing a solid, well-trained team and that is not just by chance. They’ve earned seven points away from home by beating Udinese and Venezia and drawing in Turin. They are very dangerous from set-pieces. As always, it will be up to us to have the right mentality, the desire to be on the pitch and to play at a high tempo. It will be a very tough match.”.

Despite sitting at the top of the Serie A table after 11 matches, Gattuso feels that it is still far too early to be making any sweeping predictions.

“We can only judge the standings in the last seven or eight games of the season,” he insisted. “We know these are all important matches and we have to play each one of them with the right level of respect for the opponent, then we’ll see where that takes us.

In a recent development, “I coach a team that has to take things one day at a time. It’s useless to sit there and try to make calculations. We all know the difficulties, it’s important to not make mistakes in terms of attitude or mentality.”.

After his encouraging start at the Stadio Olimpico, Gattuso was asked whether he can see himself staying put for the long term and put an end to his chopping-and-changing of clubs.

“I love going around and getting to know different cultures and mentalities,” he replied. “My growth over the last few years is a result of all the traveling I’ve done. We Italians always thin that we’re the best, but that’s absolutely not the case. If you can take something from other cultures, that’s great.

According to recent reports, “Honestly, I don’t think about whether or not I’ll be here in two or three years, I am only thinking about today and I feel comfortable here. I feel like I’ve been here for 10 years.”.

Lastly, Gattuso was asked which of Lazio’s upcoming games he feels will be the most decisive.

He responded: “I won’t answer that because there’s not a lot to say. Tomorrow’s three points are worth the same as the ones in Turin, against Atalanta or in Frosinone. They’re different opponents, but let’s think about tomorrow’s match for now.”.

#48680. Why malnutrition can go unnoticed, and what that means for our health

📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1003 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

Why malnutrition can go unnoticed, and what that means for our health

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1003 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Some 50,000 deaths can be attributed to malnutrition in Germany each year, according to the German Society for Nutritional Medicine (DGEM).
  • The problem is that malnutrition often doesn't become apparent until the consequences are already severe.
  • "In most cases, you don't notice anything at first," said Matthias Pirlich, a nutritional expert and internal medicine specialist, who once served as DGEM vice president.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Some 50,000 deaths can be attributed to malnutrition in Germany each year, according to the German Society for Nutritional Medicine (DGEM).

The problem is that malnutrition often doesn't become apparent until the consequences are already severe.

"In most cases, you don't notice anything at first," said Matthias Pirlich, a nutritional expert and internal medicine specialist, who once served as DGEM vice president. "You could have a severe vitamin D deficiency for months before any symptoms appear at all. The same applies for vitamin B12. By the time symptoms appear, such as nerve damage, it's already too late.".

According to recent reports, A long-term B12 deficiency can damage the spinal cord, leading to numbness in the limbs, muscle weakness or even paralysis. Less common deficiency-related brain damage can cause memory loss and mental health issues.

All B vitamins play an notable role in metabolism, blood formation and healthy nerve function.

Vitamins, along with various minerals such as calcium, magnesium, iron, iodine and zinc, are classed as micronutrients. The body needs to source them from food, as it cannot produce them itself. Our bodies also need macronutrients like carbohydrates, carbohydrates, protein and fats that provide us with energy.

If the body consumes less food than it needs to maintain all bodily functions over a prolonged period of time, then this is known as undernutrition. A recent World Food Organization (FAO) report estimates that approximately 645 million people worldwide suffer from chronic undernutrition.

Malnutrition, on the other hand, occurs when we consume enough calories but lack certain macronutrients or micronutrients in our food. This, too, can make one sick over time and even prove fatal. About 2 billion people worldwide suffer from this so-called hidden hunger, most of them in the Global South. That mentioned, even some people in industrialized nations lack vital micronutrients in their nutrition.

One study, for instance, found that just under three-quarters of the US population did not meet the recommended daily intake of vitamin D between 2007 and 2010, with more than two-thirds falling short of the recommended amount of vitamin E. And in Germany, about one-third of the population suffered from vitamin D deficiency in 2017, according to the German Nutrition Society. Such deficiency can cause bone, joint and muscle pain. It may also lead to an increased risk of falls and bone fractures.

In a recent development, about one-third of Germans also had an insufficient intake of iodine, a trace element that is indispensable for the production of thyroid hormones. Iodine deficiency can therefore disrupt normal thyroid function. Not only that — during pregnancy, a baby's brain and nervous system can only properly develop with an adequate supply of iodine.

The cultivation of agricultural produce with partially long shelf life or high yields has in some cases caused a decrease in the micronutrient content of fruits, vegetables and grains. Whether this drop in micronutrients is impacting human health, however, is a matter of debate.

Malnutrition can result from an unbalanced diet that, while filling and providing energy, lacks essential micronutrients. Examples of such empty calories include fast food and highly processed foods, as well as white bread and white rice.

Poverty is often the reason for such an unbalanced diet, for example when people in the Global South can only afford to buy staples such as flour or rice.

Another study found that in Germany, households at risk of poverty are more likely to consume foods that are low in nutrients and high in calories.

Sources indicate that depression is also associated with an increased risk of nutrient deficiency. "People often lose their appetite, and when they neglect their self-care, they may end up eating a very unbalanced diet," Pirlich told DW. His research shows that older adults and people who live alone often develop malnutrition, too. The risk also increases the more medications a person takes.

Many diseases result in the body being less efficient at absorbing or utilizing nutrients through the intestines. This applies to people with inflammatory or chronic disease, such as Crohn's disease, celiac disease, liver disease and cancer.

The DGEM estimates that some 30% of all patients receiving inpatient care in Germany are affected by or at risk of malnutrition. Yet health insurance data shows that only about 1% of patients are screened and treated for nutrient deficiencies.

Recent findings suggest that often, patients' malnutrition worsens during their hospital stay. The consequences can be serious, potentially causing additional complications, delayed recuperation, longer hospital stays and even increased mortality rates. This results in higher healthcare expenditure, amounting to billions each year.

It has been revealed that german policymakers and medical associations are therefore developing a initiative to better screen for and treat malnutrition in hospitals. The road map will be ready by 2027 and copy the Dutch approach in the sense that all patients are checked for nutritional deficiencies upon hospital admission.

Pirlich wants to see such screenings for at-risk groups in outpatient clinics, too: "This includes all those with chronic and serious illnesses and, above all, older adults.".

To prevent poverty-related malnutrition, Pirlich suggests increased access to healthy food, offering free school meals as an example.

According to recent reports, the nutritional expert recommends eating a diet that is varied and largely plant-based. "Secondary plant compounds have a very positive effect, and if you eat a highly diverse diet, you consume many different foods that are [nutritionally] beneficial," said Pirlich.

There's a simple rule of thumb: The more colorful your food, the better.

In a recent development, also, cook vegetables as gently as possible, because overheating and keeping them warm for too long destroys their vitamins. Long storage periods also lead to vitamin loss, so it makes sense to go for seasonal and regional foods in particular.

In a recent development, but even when ensuring a healthy and balanced diet, some people still develop a nutrient deficiency. A blood test can provide clarity, and dietary supplements may help make up for the deficiency.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Published: 16:03 EST, 20 November 2026 | Updated: 16:18 EST, 20 November 2026.

Hibernian supporters know all too well the dangers associated with getting one’s hopes up.

It’s a road they’ve been down time and time again, only to end up with that same familiar sickening feeling in the pit of their stomach at the end of it.

Which is why any talk of the Edinburgh club experiencing some sort of mini-revival should quite rightly be taken with more than a large pinch of salt.

Let’s not forget, at the start of the month, new boss Marink Reedijk had picked up a paltry point from his four games in charge since taking the reins from David Gray.

Performances weren’t up to much either.

A statement win over Hearts at Hampden to book their Premier Sports Cup final spot was backed up with an emphatic 4-0 dismantling of Aberdeen up at Pittodrie.

Hibs manager Marink Reedijk is still searching for his first victory at Easter Road.

Industry observers note that credit where it’s due, of course. Both victories were hard-earned and thoroughly deserved.

Industry observers note that but it’s important not to read too much in to either of them. Players going above and beyond in a derby clash should be a given, while the Dons appeared to have chucked it altogether under the stewardship of former manager Stephen Robinson long before Hibs turned up in the Granite City.

The real test begins this weekend with the visit of Dundee United, as Reedijk’s men look to secure a first home Premiership win in over seven months.

The fans have been crying out for entertainment in Leith for far longer than that. In the latter days of Gray’s reign, the atmosphere at Easter Road was verging on toxic.

Reedijk needs to change that, and now has two games against the Dundee clubs over the next four days to get the momentum swinging in the opposite direction.

Continuing to get the best out of his midfield three will be key to that.

The reintroduction of Joe Newell to the starting XI has paid off substantial-time. Not so much in terms of the stats, but rather what he allows Miguel Chaiwa and Josh Mulligan to do.

The former was linked with a move to Celtic over the summer, but looked miles off it in the early weeks of the campaign until Newell lined up alongside him.

Chaiwa can be guilty of trying to carry out too many jobs in the middle of the park, but Newell’s calming influence has enabled him to stick to what he’s good at — namely breaking up the play and moving the ball on to his more creative team-mates in front of him.

There’s no doubt the Zambian is at his best when he keeps things simple.

Joe Newell has provided a calming influence in the middle of the park amid this upturn in form.

Newell’s presence has also freed Mulligan to play further up the field rather than on the fringes of his own box, where he was popping up far too often a couple of months ago. He’s wasted back there.

If he can add some more goals and assists to his name over the next few, there is every chance he can play himself in to the thoughts of Scotland boss Sebastien Pocognoli ahead of the next set of internationals.

It should be an intriguing battle this afternoon in the engine room, with United boasting the most cohesive midfield group in the top flight with Dylan Tait, Lyall Cameron and Zidane Iqbal.

Of course, even if Hibs deliver in that sense, it may count for very little if the guys at the top end of the pitch can’t do the business. The lack of cutting edge has been an ongoing concern. Four goals against Aberdeen doesn't change that.

Owen Elding appears to be Reedijk’s preferred option in the central striker role, but while the young Irishman has shown flashes of his potential, he has offered little to suggest he can be relied upon to find the net on a consistent basis.

The problem is, can anyone? Record-signing Thibault Klidje may have opened his league account for the season against the Dons, however we’ve seen enough to know that he isn’t the answer.

Ante Suto is in the same boat, while Stoke City loanee Nathan Lowe has struggled for both game time and form.

And as for Rabbi Matondo? Well, the wait goes on to see any real return on that investment. Early days, mind you.

That Martin Boyle remains Hibs’ main goalscoring threat is troubling, especially given that the veteran can’t even be considered a nailed-on starter these days.

There are a significant number of players — across all areas of the park — fighting for their future at the club. Indeed, you would imagine Reedijk is counting down the days until January when he will look to freshen up the squad with guys more suited to his style.

Lyall Cameron has been a key man behind Dundee United's surge up the Premiership table.

Hibs should use today’s opponents as an example of how patience can pay off.

It’s fair to say that Jim Goodwin has never been Mr. Popular in and around Tannadice. Goodness knows why.

Many fans were calling for his head as recently as the summer after failing to secure a top-six finish last term, but he is slowly but surely starting to win over his doubters.

Make no mistake, this season presents a golden opportunity for United to seriously challenge for third spot.

You never know what you’re going to get from Hearts on any given week, while this is very much uncharted territory for Falkirk.

And let’s face it, nobody would expect the likes of Hibs, Aberdeen or Motherwell to claw themselves into contention.

While everyone else tries to stumble their way through a period of transition, United’s consistency – both on and off the park – could prove to be the difference.

Bruno Fernandes has been dropped for Manchester United’s crucial Premier League game against Bournemouth at Old Trafford on Sunday.

Michael Carrick has taken the decision to drop the United captain to the bench in the wake of his public criticism on Wednesday following the shambolic 4-1 Champions League defeat to Como.

Fernandes appeared to call out Carrick’s tactics and has now been taken out of the starting XI.

The move had looked likely with Carrick refusing to rule out stripping Fernandes of the captaincy when quizzed on the matter on Friday.

Carrick had responded to Fernandes questioning the set up and approach by suggesting tactics can go out of the window when players are unprepared to run.

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Manchester United vs Bouremouth.

In a recent development, united enter Sunday’s clash against Bournemouth in the grip of a deepening crisis. Wednesday night’s dismal 4-1 Champions League defeat to debutants Como extended United’s’ winless run to seven matches across all competitions - their worst sequence since 2015.

According to recent reports, with just one victory from their opening seven Premier League fixtures, United are enduring their worst start to a top-flight season since 1986-87. Head coach Michael Carrick, a multiple champion at Old Trafford during his playing days, finds his position under severe threat, with reports suggesting another defeat could seal his departure. While both of United’s wins this season have come at home, they remain winless in their last three at Old Trafford. On an individual level, Bryan Mbeumo has offered a rare bright spark, scoring four goals in seven league outings while Bruno Fernandes continues to search for form, and the captain’s recent outburst only makes the atmosphere more febrile.

In a recent development, in stark contrast, Bournemouth arrive in Manchester brimming with confidence. Marco Rose’s side have enjoyed a flawless start to their inaugural European campaign, sitting joint-top of the Europa League standings after a dominant 3-0 victory over Ruben Amorim’s ten-man AC Milan on Thursday. That result marked a third consecutive home win and clean sheet, with Bournemouth outscoring opponents 8-0 in that stretch. Midfielder Marcus Tavernier has been instrumental, leading the club’s scoring charts with five goals across 11 appearances.

Bournemouth will feel no trepidation visiting Old Trafford, having gone unbeaten in their last six Premier League meetings with United (two wins, four draws). With Carrick desperate for a stabilising result and Rose’s side riding high on European momentum, today’s fixture carries significant stakes for both clubs.
